newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Handover stirs fear, hope among Hong Kong artists.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Handover stirs fear, hope among Hong Kong artists.

text.p: In a city where for many years the two main preoccupations were getting rich and getting out, the arts in Hong Kong were often relegated to backstage.

But the 1980s and 1990s have seen a transformation in a place once dismissed as a cultural desert just as the British colony faces an unsettling challenge posed by the handover to China in the middle of next year.
But where some see gloom ahead, others see opportunities, both for Hong Kong to gain stature as a gateway to China and for the territory's people to establish their own identity.
Oscar Ho, director of exhibitions at Hong Kong's independent Arts Centre, is one of those who see the potential for a type of renaissance in the meeting of the two Chinese cultures.

"I'm not trying to romanticise it...but I think it's better than before when we lived in this kind of wishy-washy, ambiguous existence, this kind of most-laughable label called East meets West," Ho said in an interview.
"There's still a lot of anxiety...about regression socially and politically," Ho said, but added: "Culturally I have never been more optimistic.

"International interest artistically gives Hong Kong artists more maturity and...it's more exciting because becoming part of a strong, powerful culture, we are suddenly being forced to ask, what does it mean to be Hong Kong Chinese?"
Tang Shu-wing, an actor and director who is among many artists to have forged strong ties with mainland colleagues, agrees.

"There is a fear of loss of liberty, of freedom of expression. On the other hand it's the first time in my life that we are facing (the prospect of being) a country," he said. "This is quite challenging as an artist."

Hong Kong's artistic community shares the hope China will live up to its pledge that the territory will continue to enjoy its considerable freedoms for 50 years after the handover under the "one country, two systems" formula drawn up by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
But some say the heavy hand of Beijing is already being felt.
The Chinese government wanted advance lists and screenings of films to be shown at Hong Kong's annual Film Festival earlier this year, sources close to the organisers said.
The Urban Council refused.
A film critic with close connections to the festival said pressure to toe the political line was certain to increase once Beijing was in charge.
"I don't think they would stop the festival, that would be too stupid, too clumsy," he said, asking not to be named. "But subtly, there are things they can do."
The important thing was for organisers to continue to act independently even if pressure is applied.

Artists fear one avenue of influence would be to target the the Urban Council, or local council, which runs the film festival and is a major donor of money and venues to almost every arts endeavour in Hong Kong.

Ada Wong, vice chairman of the council's culture select committee, said she and her colleagues had to work on the assumption the council would be allowed to continue to fund the arts without interference from Beijing.
She said her committee had felt no direct pressure so far.
"What we believe in is a smooth transition... I'm sure we will have a strong enough voice (to have influence with Beijing)," she said. "Let's hope so."
Organisers of the Arts Festival, Hong Kong's showpiece annual arts extravaganza, say they have not encountered overt pressure and don't expect to after 1997.

Grace Lang, the festival's programme director, preferred to concentrate on Hong Kong's key role in helping mainland artists find funding, venues and international recognition, especially at a time when China is privatising its state-run troupes.

"Hong Kong provides a platform," she said. "We as promoters have a responsibility of promoting them in a way which is actually helping them. And not to make statements which would bring negative effects."
Other arts professionals are more gloomy although none of them say they have proof of interference.
Such situations have already put Hong Kong's artists and arts organisers in an awkward position, having to guess at what might be considered sensitive by a future government.

"You don't know how it will be viewed next year," said one organiser, who admitted he found himself deliberately playing down the political overtones of a recent event even though he had not received any pressure to do so.
"This kind of ambiguity will last for a long time."
